1:
With Eliphaz silenced, the second of Job's three friends rises to take up the charge, and the witnesses gather first around the man and the manner of his coming. The reformed John Gill introduces Bildad the Shuhite as one who had agreed beforehand with his companions upon both the side they should take and the part each should bear, the general sentiment being the same in them all; and he catches the discourtesy of the entrance in a memorable figure — Job's friends were like the messengers who brought the tidings of his losses, for before one had done speaking another came, so that no sooner had Eliphaz finished than Bildad started up to charge him afresh. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the man's pedigree, taking him for a descendant of Shuah, one of the sons of Abraham by Keturah, who dwelt in Arabia Deserta, the land called in Scripture the east country (Gen. 25:2); and he lays out the plan of the whole speech — that God is just and never punishes but for iniquity, that Job's children were cut off for their sin, that humble submission would restore an innocent man, and that the fate of the wicked, drawn from the vegetable world, shows how soon their hope must perish.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the harshness of the opening. Bildad begins self-confidently with a quousque tandem, a peremptory "how long," and the word rendered "these things" means not "this" but "of such kind" — speeches which, in their emptiness, are like the wind, and, in their vehemence, like a boisterous wind; for Bildad sees in them the justice of the Absolute One impugned, and cannot bear that it should be so much as questioned.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the friend more searchingly. Bildad reproves Job and checks his passion, but, as is too common, with a greater passion of his own, taking it for granted that Eliphaz had already said enough to silence him and so treating all Job's reply as impertinent — "reproofs," Henry observes with Caryl, "are often grounded upon mistakes," men's meaning not being taken aright, and they gravely rebuked as if they were evil-doers. Henry grants that Bildad is right in the main thesis, that God does not pervert judgment, for shall not the Judge of all the earth do right (Gen. 18:25)? Yet he is not fair in the application, dragging in the death of Job's children as though the manner of their end proved them sinners above all others. So the witnesses set the frame for the chapter: a new accuser, orthodox in his creed and unkind in his charge, who will build a true doctrine into a false indictment.
2:
Bildad's opening sentence falls as a rebuke of Job's very speech — "how long wilt thou speak these things? and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?" — and the witnesses weigh both the impatience of the question and the force of its figure. The reformed John Gill hears several tempers in the words at once: Bildad may be wondering that a man so wasted in body and depressed in spirit should be able to keep up so vehement a discourse; or angry at what he took for blasphemy against God and a charging of him with unrighteousness; or impatient of Job's long reply, breaking in before he had well finished, that he might return an answer of his own; or plainly despising the whole as idle talk, so that some render the taunt, "how long wilt thou trifle after this manner?"

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the image in the Hebrew. The phrase is poetical, a "mighty wind," the same word for the great wind that smote the house in ch. 1:19; Bildad means that Job's speeches are like the wind in their nothingness and like a boisterous wind in their vehemence, sound and fury signifying, to his ear, no truth at all.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen the accusation into a syllogism. Adam Clarke reads the charge as, "how long wilt thou go on to charge God foolishly?" — for in Bildad's logic the heavy affliction proves Job under the divine wrath, and that wrath, thus manifested, proves that it is for his sins that God punishes him. On the figure Clarke prefers the Arabic and Syriac, which read not "strong wind" but "the spirit of pride," so that the sense becomes, "wilt thou continue to breathe forth a tempest of words?" John Wesley keeps the received image and gives it its plainest weight — the strong wind is speech "boisterous and violent," blustering and dangerous.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the taunt a pointed retort. Job had already excused his own vehemence by pleading that his speeches were but as wind, that his friends should not make so much ado about them (ch. 6:26); "yea, but," says Bildad in effect, they are as a strong wind, blustering and threatening, boisterous and dangerous, and therefore we are concerned to fence against them. The witnesses do not divide over the substance: whether the wind is emptiness, violence, or pride, all agree that Bildad opens not by weighing Job's grief but by dismissing his words, so assured of his own cause that he counts the sufferer's cry mere bluster to be fenced against rather than a wound to be understood. It is an entrance, they leave us feeling, that answers a broken man's argument with a slammed door.
3:
"Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice?" — Bildad's doubled question is the axle on which his whole speech turns, and the witnesses read it as a truth rightly held and wrongly aimed. The reformed John Gill sets Bildad squarely over against Job, whom he supposes to have charged God with injustice in his dealings with himself and his children; and the two clauses, he notes, say the same thing twice for emphasis — the answer to both is a resounding No. God does not pervert judgment; far be it from him, and far be it from us to suspect it. The repetition is not idle: it presses the point home that the fault, wherever it lies, cannot lie with the Judge.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lingers, as often, over the divine names, and finds a whole argument folded into them. The verse calls God first by the name of might, the strong or all-sufficient God, and then by the name of the Almighty; and these titles, Wesley says, are emphatically used to prove that God cannot deal unjustly or falsely with men, because he has no need of it and no temptation to it — being self-sufficient for his own happiness, and able by his own invincible power to do whatsoever pleases him. Men pervert justice out of fear or for gain; but God, who fears none and can be bribed by none, is under no such pressure, so that to "pervert" judgment would be inconsistent both with his nature and with his office as governor of the world.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the same principle straight against Job with a colder edge. "God afflicts thee," he has Bildad reason; "can he afflict thee for naught? As he is just, his judgment is just; and he could not inflict punishment unless there be a cause." Here is the exact hinge of the friends' error laid bare — the leap from the certainty that God is righteous to the false certainty that every sufferer must be guilty. The witnesses do not contend with the doctrine, which they hold as firmly as Bildad does; their reserve is all for its use. That the Almighty does no wrong is the surest of truths; but Bildad turns it into a probe for hidden sin, and so makes a sound premise the first step of a cruel inference, as though the very justice of God required that Job's ashes be read as the wages of some concealed transgression.
4:
Bildad's proof of divine justice fastens at once on the freshest of Job's wounds, arguing that "if thy children have sinned against him," God has but given them over to the hand of their own transgression; and here the witnesses divide sharply over whether the manner of the children's death may be read as the measure of their guilt. The reformed John Gill reports the friend's reasoning and half goes along with it — the children had no doubt sinned, and, as Bildad thought, in a very notorious manner, and so were righteously punished, this being produced as the proof that God does not pervert but executes justice. Gill notes the pliancy of the opening particle, which may be rendered "if," "seeing," "because," or "though," and cites Broughton's blunt turn, "as thy children have sinned against him, so hath he sent them into the hand of their trespass" — a righteous retaliation.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke voices Bildad's inference more plainly still: "I know thy children have been cut off by a terrible judgment; but was it not because by transgression they had filled up the measure of their iniquity?" To be "cast away," he adds with the Targum, is to be sent off to the place of their transgression, to the punishment their sins had earned. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps to the grammar, rendering the clause literally "then he sent them away," so that it was by means of their own transgression that their destruction came.

Against all this the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry enters the great protest. Job readily owned that God does not pervert judgment; but it does not therefore follow either that his children were cast-aways or that they died for some extraordinary sin. It is true that we and our children have sinned, and must justify God in all he brings upon us; yet extraordinary afflictions are not always the punishment of extraordinary sins, but are sometimes the trial of extraordinary graces, and in judging another's case, unless the contrary appears, we ought to take the more favourable side, as our Saviour directs (Luke 13:2-4). "Here Bildad missed it." So the verse opens a genuine debate that the whole book will prosecute: whether a shocking providence is proof of a special guilt (v.3), as Bildad urges and Gill and Clarke report, or whether the innocent may be as heavily stricken as the guilty, so that the death of Job's children convicts them of nothing.
5:
From the dead children Bildad turns to the living father, and his tone appears for a moment to soften into counsel: "if thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty." The reformed John Gill hears the shift and reads a tacit distinction in it — Job is spared where his children were not, and so may yet, by applying himself to God and living a godly life, be restored to his former or to better circumstances. To seek God "betimes," Gill explains with the Hebrew, is to seek him in the morning, in the first place and above all things, taking the first opportunity without delay and with the whole heart, for God is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same word: it is to "rise early" to seek him, speedily, early, and diligently.

The other wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, catches the barbed comfort in the offer. God has afflicted thee severely and removed thy children by a terrible judgment; yet in that very sparing of thyself lies a proof, Bildad urges, that "he waits to be gracious to thee" — humble thyself before him, implore his mercy, and thou shalt be saved.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees clearly that the counsel is the very same Eliphaz had already given (ch. 5:8), and suspects Bildad of offering it without expecting Job to take it — meaning, that is, to condemn him, while wishing to be thought to comfort him. Yet the advice is good in itself: to seek God not with complaint but with petition, in humility and faith, with sincerity in the heart and honesty in the house, since it is only the prayer of the upright that prevails (Prov. 15:8), and a heart that regards iniquity God will not hear (Ps. 66:18). The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the construction — "to turn oneself to God earnestly seeking," a pregnant phrase like the "seeking unto God" Eliphaz had used before — and read the clause that follows, "the habitation of thy righteousness," as the home God would care for and restore once a man had shown himself, though not suffering undeservedly, yet pure and upright in his inmost mind. The witnesses converge on the double edge of the appeal: the road Bildad points out is the right one, prayer and humble submission to the God who afflicts, and the counsel to seek him early is no worse for being urgent; yet he points it out as one still convinced that only a secret sinner could be lying where Job lies, so that the very door he opens toward mercy he opens with a hand that presses guilt upon the man he bids walk through it.
6:
The condition grows more pointed as Bildad names the terms of Job's recovery — "if thou wert pure and upright, surely now he would awake for thee" — and the witnesses hear beneath the promise an insinuation that Job is neither. The reformed John Gill owns the sting: by the very "if," Bildad tacitly intimates that Job is not pure in heart nor upright in life, though the book itself, and God's own testimony, had pronounced him perfect and upright. Gill will not let the slur stand unanswered on its own ground, and turns the words toward the gospel — no man is pure of himself, nor any so pure as to be free from sin; but those are pure in heart who have clean hearts created in them and their consciences sprinkled and purified by faith in the blood of Christ, and in that sense Job, having an interest in a living Redeemer, was pure indeed.

The grammatical-historical witnesses read the clause as Bildad's own logic laid bare. Charles Ellicott states it without softening: "Of course, then, there is but one inference: thou art not pure and upright. These are verily the wounds of a friend which are not faithful." Bildad, he observes, wishes to be very orthodox, to base his statements upon authority, and so he calls up the experience of former ages and, like Eliphaz, has recourse to figures — only his figures are highly obscure. He contemplates the two representative characters of the whole book, the righteous and the wicked, and paints the wicked first under the likeness of the paper-reed that grows in the mire of Egyptian swamps: surrounded with moisture, yet liable soon to wither, so the wicked man withers in the midst of abundance. Keil and Delitzsch add that Bildad's appeal to the fathers calls to mind the charge of Deut. 32:7, "remember the days of old."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the whole verse into irony, and finds the cruelty of it in the phrase "the habitation of thy righteousness." Concerning thy guilt, he has Bildad imply, there can be no doubt; for hadst thou been holy, would not God long ere this have manifested his power in thy behalf, punished thine enemies, and restored thee? And "the habitation of thy righteousness" is strongly ironical — if thy house had been as a temple of God, its worship kept and his commandments obeyed, would it now lie in ruin and desolation? John Wesley keeps the plainer sense, taking the habitation for the concerns of Job's house and family, got and managed with righteousness. The witnesses converge on the barb they all detect: a fair-sounding "if" that quietly assumes the worst, offering hope with one hand while withdrawing Job's integrity with the other.
7:
Bildad crowns his conditional promise with a future out of all proportion to the past — "though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase" — and the witnesses read it both as prophecy and, unwittingly, as a thing God would literally fulfil. The reformed John Gill takes the "beginning" first of Job's original estate, which had grown until he was the greatest man in all the east, yet was small compared with what a restored man might enjoy; and then, more aptly, of a fresh and lowly new start, for at present Job had nothing at all to begin with. He cites Broughton's turn, "thy former state should be little to thy latter," and marks the strange accuracy of the word, since Job was in the end given double all that he had lost.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it in the same key of extravagant increase. Thy former prosperity, he has Bildad promise, would be small beside that into which God would bring thee; for to show his respect for a piety that had suffered the loss of all things, he would multiply thy former estate until thou hadst far more than ever thou didst possess. The promise, in Bildad's mouth, is conditional upon a repentance he doubts Job can produce; but the witnesses cannot help noting how the event overtook the theory.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the law of growth hidden in the line, and turns it from a taunt into a comfort. This, he says, is God's way of enriching the souls of his people with graces and comforts — not per saltum, as by a sudden bound, but per gradum, step by step: the beginning is small, but the progress is toward perfection. Dawning light grows to noonday, and a grain of mustard seed to a great tree; let us not therefore despise the day of small things (Zech. 4:10), but hope for the day of great things. So the schools converge on a promise whose form is sound even where its aim is false: whether Job begins again with a little meal in the barrel or with nothing in his hand, the God who blesses can multiply the smallest remnant to a great increase — a truth Bildad wields as a lure to repentance, and which Job's own restored fortune would one day prove, to the confusion of the very argument that here advanced it.
8:
For the authority behind his doctrine Bildad sends Job back past the living to the dead — "inquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers" — and the witnesses attend both to the appeal and to the wisdom it claims. The reformed John Gill explains that Bildad does not ask Job to take his word, but to learn from history how it has always fared: good men afflicted and behaving well have been delivered and left more flourishing than before, as Noah, Abraham, and Lot; while the wicked and the hypocrite, flourish as they may for a season, have perished utterly, as the descendants of Cain, the builders of Babel, and the men of Sodom. The "former age," Gill insists against the Septuagint, is not the first age of the world but the generations gone before, whose records repay the searching.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear in the summons an echo of Moses' charge to remember the days of old (Deut. 32:7), and read "the search of their fathers" as the collected result of the ancients' inquiry — the profound wisdom gathered from long experience, to which our own ephemeral and shadowy life is no fit substitute for judging the dealings of God. The wesleyan-arminian voices press the reach of the appeal: Adam Clarke takes "the former age" of the first generation of men, the patriarchs, so that Bildad points to an antiquity exceedingly remote; and John Wesley glosses the "search" as a serious and industrious ransacking of the ancient records.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the fullest reading, and quietly Christianizes the method. Bildad, he says, insists not on his own judgment, owning that "we are but of yesterday, and know nothing," and so refers the matter to the testimony of the ancients, who lived nearer the fountain-head of revelation and long enough to observe the ways of Providence. Yet Henry adds the reformer's correction: blessed be God, now that we have his word in writing and are directed to search that, we need not inquire of the former age, for the Scripture is as near to us as it was to them (Rom. 10:8), and by keeping God's precepts we may understand more than the ancients (Ps. 119:99). He will not go so far as Eliphaz, who had asked whoever perished being innocent (ch. 4:7); but he grants that if we take in the other world, it is an undoubted truth that the hopes of the hypocrite come at last to ruin. The witnesses converge: Bildad's appeal to antiquity is sound as far as it reaches, and reaches, in the event, further than he knew.
9:
The reason for consulting the fathers rather than the friends is Bildad's own confessed smallness — "for we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow" — and the witnesses linger over the humility and the arithmetic of the line. The reformed John Gill is careful not to press "yesterday" too literally: it means a short space of time backward, and especially so when set against the antediluvian fathers, the greater part of whom lived upwards of nine hundred years. Bildad and his companions were themselves no striplings but men well advanced in years, gray-headed and older than Job's own father, as Eliphaz had boasted when he set the aged on his side; yet beside those long-lived patriarchs of the world before the flood, whose centuries gave them room to watch the ways of God, their whole generation is but of yesterday, a thing of a single day's standing.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke builds the same contrast into an argument about knowledge. Those earlier men, from a lifespan of eight or nine hundred years, had opportunity to make many observations and treasure up a vast fund of experience; measured against them the present age is as nothing, a generation of yesterday, its days a mere shadow. Clarke cannot resist the emblem: he recalls the shadow cast by the gnomon of a sundial, and the motto he had seen graven on one — Umbrae sumus, "We are shadows" — for as a single solar day, so is our life, fleeting and unsubstantial; and he hears behind the verse David's confession that "our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is none abiding" (1 Chron. 29:15). John Wesley reduces it to its plain sense: being but lately born, we have little knowledge and experience, and live not long enough to make sound observations on the methods of divine Providence.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the hinge on which Bildad's figures will turn, for having pleaded the shortness of life he now likens the prosperity of the godless to the deceitful ground on which a papyrus or reed springs up quickly and as quickly withers, wanting perpetual water. The witnesses do not divide; they hear Bildad turn a genuine and even attractive modesty — the confession that a shadow cannot judge the eternal — into the ground of an argument from tradition, humble in its premise yet, as the chapter will show, unbending in the use he makes of it against a suffering friend.
10:
Having owned the ignorance of his own generation, Bildad promises Job better teachers in the fathers — "shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart?" — and the witnesses dwell on the weight of that word from the heart. The reformed John Gill explains the confidence simply: the men of the former age, and their fathers before them, are the ones Job is directed to inquire of and to prepare to search, and from them he might reasonably expect to be taught and told things very instructive to his present case. The knowledge Bildad offers is not his own but a borrowed and elder wisdom, handed down and, he assumes, decisive.

The wesleyan-arminian voices bring out the reverence and the sincerity the verse claims for that teaching. Adam Clarke turns the questions into an exhortation — wilt thou not treat their maxims with the utmost deference and respect? — and finds in "words out of their heart" the mark of their trustworthiness: what they say is the fruit of long and careful experience, not the guess of a moment. John Wesley unfolds the phrase clause by clause: the fathers utter their words "not partially, but sincerely," speaking their inward thoughts; "not rashly, but from deep consideration"; and "not by hearsay, but by their own knowledge" — three notes of a testimony that carries authority because it comes from within.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very brevity of the verse invites them to reflect on what makes any teaching go home. Bildad's assumption is that the settled voice of antiquity, spoken from the heart of men who had watched the world long, must silence a sufferer's complaint; and there is a truth in it that the witnesses will not deny, for words that come from the heart of the teacher are likeliest to reach the heart of the learner, and experience honestly gathered is a treasure worth the search. Yet the same witnesses have already hinted at the flaw folded into so fair a principle. The wisdom of the fathers is real, but Bildad has decided in advance what it must say — that calamity spells guilt — and so the appeal to hearts full of experience becomes, in his hand, a way of overbearing the one heart before him whose experience most needed to be heard. The teachers are good; the use he will make of them is not yet just.
11:
"Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?" — with this first of his borrowed similitudes Bildad likens the hypocrite's hope to a marsh-plant that cannot live a moment cut off from its wet ground, and the witnesses work at both the botany and the barb. The reformed John Gill takes the "rush" for the bulrush, which delights in watery places and draws its very name in Hebrew from its drinking up of water, thriving only in moist and marshy clay; and he reports the Septuagint's identification of it with the paper-reed that grows in the fenlands of Egypt beside the still waters of the Nile.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes the plant certain. The word gome, he says, is beyond doubt the Egyptian flag, the papyrus on which the ancients wrote and from which our very word "paper" descends; the Septuagint translators, working in Egypt and perhaps writing on the very substance in question, rendered it papyros, "can the papyrus flourish without water?" — a version that leaves the meaning in no doubt. Clarke sets the elaborate Latin of Linnaeus beside the plain description of the old herbalist John Gerarde to show how the plant rises six or seven cubits above the muddy banks of the Nile, and needs an abundance of water for its nourishment; the "flag," he adds, is likely the reed that Hasselquist found by the same river, whose leaves the Egyptians lay in water like hemp and then work into good and strong cables, so that the very name may take its rise, like the word for a brother, from the joining and associating of many threads into one.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies the flag more precisely still as the plant of Pharaoh's meadow, on which the cattle fed in the dream of Gen. 41:2, and notes that Bildad's figure will presently be reinforced by a second, the spider's web, the most fragile and transient of tenements. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the moral the plant is made to carry: the hypocrite can no more build his hope without some false and rotten ground to raise it from than the rush can grow without mire or the flag without water. So the witnesses converge on Bildad's point while genuinely dividing over his plant — bulrush, papyrus, or Nile-reed — agreeing that whatever green thing he means, its lesson is the same: a confidence rooted only in the marsh of outward prosperity must perish the instant its water fails.
12:
The very speed with which the marsh-plant shoots up is turned by Bildad into the sign of its ruin — "whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb." The reformed John Gill fixes the moment: before the plant has come to its full height or proper ripeness, before it has so much as flowered, being without moisture or watery clay, it changes and fades. It is not felled by any hand; it dies of itself, and dies early, so that its very freshness is deceptive, a greenness already doomed.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the suddenness of the decay. Adam Clarke, owning that we do not know enough of the plant's natural history to feel the full force of the figure, gathers that this succulent reed, for all its quick and luxuriant growth, is short-lived and speedily withers — perhaps in the dry season, or on the retreat of the waters of the Nile — and sums it in the horticultural maxim, "Soon ripe, soon rotten." John Wesley draws out the irony of the greenness: it is the very thing that "promises long continuance," and yet, though no man cut it down, it withers of itself, and withers sooner than the hardier herbs around it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch remind the reader that the plant is never the true subject: throughout these lines it is not the creeping reed directly but the ungodly man likened to it, so that the expression runs half figurative and half literal, the image bending always back toward its meaning. The withering reed is the prosperity of the godless, green today and gone tomorrow.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the strangeness of a death without a stroke. The rush, he observes, may look green and gay for a while, and even outgrow the grass, but it is light and hollow and empty, green only for show and of no real use; and it withers presently, before any other herb — even while it is in its greenness it is already going. There lies its difference from the common grass: the grass is cut down and then withers (Ps. 90:6), but the rush is not cut down, and yet withers, withers before it is grown up (Ps. 129:6), so that as it has no use it has no continuance. The witnesses do not divide; they let the figure make its own quiet, alarming point, that the worst state of the hypocrite and the evil-doer borders always upon withering — that even when his profession is greenest it is already going, cut off by no visible stroke but by the failure of the hidden ground it stood in. There is no need of an axe where there is no root of water; the plant that outgrew the grass is undone precisely by the haste that made it seem so full of life.
13:
The reed's silent death becomes Bildad's parable of a whole class of men — "so are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish" — and the witnesses read the two clauses as one sentence of doom. The reformed John Gill unfolds the forgetting: these are men who forget that there is a God, who is not in all their thoughts; who forget the works of creation and providence in which he is displayed; who forget the daily benefits of his goodness and are not thankful; who forget his word and worship, and follow after lying vanities. Such men, like the bulrush and the flag, are unfruitful and unprofitable, standing in the mire and clay of an unregenerate state, and however high they may carry their heads in a fair profession, when tribulation arises their greenness fails.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke ties the figure back to its ground: the papyrus and the rush flourish only while they have a plentiful supply of ooze and water, and take these away and their prosperity is quickly at an end; so the wicked and profane, whatever their present show, are soon dried up from the very roots. But Clarke pauses here over a single word, and enters a genuine dissent from the common rendering. This, he notes, is the first place where the term translated "hypocrite" occurs, the Hebrew chaneph, which properly conveys pollution and defilement rather than hypocrisy; and he argues that "hypocrite" is a poor translation, for a hypocrite, conscious of his insincerity, could have no real hope, whereas the man in the text plainly has hope — as all the vile and profligate do, hoping to end their sins before they end their lives, and to reach heaven at the last. The word, he insists, names the polluted, not merely the pretender.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley guards the sense of "paths" against a natural misreading: by the paths of such men Bildad does not mean their manner of living but the events that befall them, God's manner of dealing with them — the road their fortunes travel, which ends in the withering just described. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the root of the whole: forgetfulness of God lies at the bottom of men's hypocrisy and of the vain hopes with which they flatter themselves, for men would not deceive themselves so if they did not forget that God searches the heart and will not be mocked. The witnesses converge on the ruin of a hope with no root — Clarke alone lingering to correct the name we give the man who nurses it.
14:
Bildad presses the parable to its breaking-point, drawing out the frailty of the thing the ungodly leans on — "whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web." The reformed John Gill notes that the first clause repeats the doom of the verse before for the certainty of it: the hope shall be of no manner of use, wholly lost, and issue in black despair. He finds a further colour in the Hebrew, which carries the sense of loathing, so that the line may be read "whom his hope shall loathe," or "who shall loathe his hope" — the man at last fretting and vexing himself that he should have been such a fool as to place his confidence in so vain a thing, and finding himself most sadly disappointed.

The wesleyan-arminian voices fasten on the gossamer image. Adam Clarke pictures such men, subdued by the strong habits of sin, hoping on fruitlessly until the last thread of the web of life is cut off from the beam, and then finding no more strength in their hope than there is in the threads of a spider's web; the foundation on which they trust is rotten, and Mr. Good's rendering, "thus shall their support rot away," catches it exactly, the whole superstructure of their confidence tumbling into ruin. John Wesley takes the "hope" concretely for the man's wealth and outward glory, the very matter of his trust, which shall be cut off suddenly and violently taken away; and the "web," he adds, though it be formed with great art and industry, is easily swept down or pulled in pieces.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the comparison its sharpest edge. The hope of the hypocrite, he says, is woven out of his own bowels, spun from a false conceit of his own merit and sufficiency, as the spider draws her web from herself; there is all the difference in the world between the work of the bee, which fetches in its sweetness from the flowers, and the work of the spider, which spins its snare out of nothing but itself. And such a web, however cunningly wrought, will be swept away in a moment when God comes to purge his house, so that when a wicked man dies his expectation perishes with him. The witnesses do not divide; they leave the ungodly clinging to a thread of his own spinning, and name the certainty that it will not bear his weight.
15:
Bildad follows the spider into its own house to show how the trust betrays the truster — "he shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand; he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure." The reformed John Gill reads the house as whatever the man makes the ground of his confidence, which is but a spider's house at best: his riches and outward prosperity, from which he concludes himself high in God's favour, or his works of righteousness and round of external duties, in which he wraps himself as in a web. To lean and to hold fast upon such a thing, Gill says, is to make flesh his arm, to lean upon a broken reed, to build a house upon the sand — a security that gives way the moment it is trusted.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prizes the exactness of the natural image, and claims to have watched it. The allusion is to the spider itself, which, suspecting its web to be frail, leans upon it here and there, propping itself on its hinder legs and pulling with its fore claws to test whether all be safe; where it finds the web injured it adds new cordage and fastens it to the wall, and then, satisfied, retires into its hole in a corner as if in complete security — when in a moment the brush or the besom sweeps away itself, its house, and its confidence together. So the wicked man, whose hope is in his temporal possessions, keeps his house in repair and leans upon his earthly supports, until the blast of God's judgments overwhelms house and man at once. It is a very fine and expressive metaphor, Clarke adds, which not one of the commentators he had seen ever discovered.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks with a single stroke that "the description of the wicked man ends here," so that the whole reed-and-spider parable closes on this collapsing house. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the "house" more widely as all that Scripture gathers under the word — a man's children, servants, and wealth, on which he trusts to uphold himself; but that web, "that refuge of lies," will be swept away, and he crushed in it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already caught the same picture, of the formal professor who leans on his web, pleases himself in it, and takes hold with his hands as the spider that is in kings' palaces (Prov. 30:28), only to have it fail him when he most needs it. The witnesses agree: the surest-seeming refuge of the godless is precisely the one that will not stand.
16:
A new and heartier image now rises in Bildad's speech — "he is green before the sun, and his branch shooteth forth in his garden" — and here the witnesses divide most sharply, over whether this flourishing plant is still the wicked man or someone else entirely. The reformed John Gill, with the majority, reads it as a tall and vigorous tree to which the hypocrite in his most prosperous circumstances is compared, green in its leaves and beautiful to look on, full of sap and juice — his profession like green leaves without fruit, a fair show in the flesh that will yet come to nothing. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same way: the wicked is a luxuriant plant in a good soil and a good situation, well exposed to the sun, its roots twining among the stones for stability, until suddenly an unknown blast strikes it and it dies from the root; he had often, he says, seen sound and healthy trees so struck, and prosperous sinners likewise blasted and stripped in the inscrutable providence of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry joins them, likening the secure and prosperous sinner to a green bay-tree (Ps. 37:35), fixed and deep-rooted, growing in firm ground and not in mire, as Nebuchadnezzar saw himself in the great tree of his dream (Dan. 4:10) — allowed every advantage he could desire, only to be suddenly cut off; and John Wesley agrees that the man who thinks himself wronged to be compared to a mere rush may be compared instead to a flourishing, well-rooted tree, green and public in the view of all men, his branches his very children, set in the most desirable circumstances — and yet suddenly cut off. Keil and Delitzsch too keep the ungodly as the subject throughout.

Against this consensus the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets a dissenting reading. Here, as he understands it, begins another and an opposite picture, marked in the Hebrew by an emphatic pronoun: "green is he," and green in a truer way than the watery paper-reed, verdant and luxuriant not in the midst of moisture but even before the sun, with not the same mere promise of verdure but a greater realisation of it. Ellicott points back to the pure and upright man of v.6, and floats the possibility that Bildad now contrasts the genuinely flourishing with the sham. So the debate is real: is the green tree of these verses the hypocrite given every advantage and still destroyed, as Gill, Clarke, Henry, Wesley, and Keil and Delitzsch all hold, or an emphatically different figure, the truly rooted man set over against the withering reed, as Ellicott alone proposes?
17:
The tree's very rootage is made to tell the story of a false security — "his roots are wrapped about the heap, and seeth the place of stones." The reformed John Gill reads the heap as a heap of stones about which the tree twists and interlaces its roots, securing itself and growing on in spite of them; and in this he sees the seeming stability of the hypocrite, who not only flourishes but appears to take root, and maintains his ground amid difficulties — like the seed sown on stony places, that springs up bravely and has no depth of earth. The strength is genuine to the eye, and altogether deceptive.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same roots the opposite way, as the secret of a real and lasting vigour. They are wrapped about the stones because from below they draw moisture, planted near a perennial fountain that fertilises them underneath, which is why the tree is green before the sun; and the phrase rendered "the place of stones" he takes rather as "the house of stones" — the permanent, durable edifice of stone, the habitation of settled civilisation, upon which the tree looks and to which it clings. His holding is so firm that even if it be plucked up, its roots and suckers are so numerous that they leave descendants behind, so that out of its earth, or out of another soil, others grow, and the transplanted tree flourishes still. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps to the plainer note of strength: the detail of the stony heap is added to signify the tree's firmness, that it stood not in loose and sandy ground which a violent wind might overthrow, but in solid earth, its numerous and spreading roots embracing the very stones and taking the advantage of the place to strengthen itself.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to where all this is tending, observing that the close of Bildad's speech sounds quite like the Psalms, and glossing the promise soon to come — that God is ready to "take by the hand" the man who is his own, as the Lord holds the right hand of his servant in Isa. 41:13. The witnesses do not finally divide over the fact that the tree seems securely fixed; their difference is over what that fixity means — to Gill and Wesley a false stability soon to be exposed, to Ellicott a genuine rootage in perennial springs and enduring stone. Either way the verse sets the stage for the sudden overthrow the next line will spring.
18:
"If he destroy him from his place" — and with that stroke the flourishing tree of the preceding verses is torn up, its very ground disowning it: "then it shall deny him, saying, I have not seen thee." The reformed John Gill offers several turns of the picture. The sun, having risen in its heat, may strike the tree until it withers and perishes from the spot where it grew; or the tree may be rooted up outright, as the Targum has it; or, dropping the figure, God may destroy the hypocrite from his place, removing him out of the garden which is the church, detested and rejected by good men, or stripping him of the honour, credit, and esteem he had among men, or cutting him down out of the world altogether as a cumberer of the ground.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the line a plain reference to the loss of an inheritance, and delights in the bold personification of the second clause. God destroys the man from his estate; it passes into the hands of another; and when he revisits the place, the ground itself, by a striking figure, says to him, "I know thee not; I have never seen thee." This too, Clarke adds soberly, he had witnessed in life — a man's holding lost, the very fields that had been his refusing to own him. John Wesley reads the actors of the verse straightforwardly: it is God who destroys, the God who is at once the saviour of good men and the destroyer of the wicked; and it is "the place" to which the denying and the seeing are figuratively ascribed, so that the man shall be so utterly extirpated that there is no memorial of him left.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the image into his theme of the sinner felled and forgotten. The tree, so fair and firmly rooted, is destroyed from his place and so entirely rooted out that no sign or token remains where it grew; the very place says, "I have not seen thee," and the standers-by say the same — "I sought him, but he could not be found" (Ps. 37:36). He made a great show and a great noise for a time, Henry says, but he is gone of a sudden, and neither root nor branch is left him (Mal. 4:1). The witnesses do not divide; whether the destroyer be named the sun, the Targum's uprooting hand, or God himself, they agree that the end of the prosperous wicked is a place swept so clean that it forgets he was ever there.
19:
"Behold, this is the joy of his way" — Bildad points, with heavy irony, to the sum of all the hypocrite's flourishing, and the witnesses catch the bitterness in it. The reformed John Gill reads the "joy" as the short-lived exultation of the man in his prosperity, a joy but for a moment, which now issues in this — entire destruction from his place; the "behold" is set before it to mark how strange and worthy of notice the reversal is, and to seal its certainty. Gill allows, as a second possibility, that the words might be turned upon good men, whose joy in believing survives every earthly loss and is perfected when they are transplanted from earth to heaven; but the plain drift is the mocking epitaph of the wicked.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the line as strong irony indeed: here is the issue of all his mirth, his sports and games and pastimes — the domineering, polluted scape-grace levelled at last with those he had despised, brought to cringe for a morsel of bread or to end his days in a workhouse; "this also," Clarke says, "I have most literally witnessed." And "out of the earth shall others grow" he takes as the plainest sequel: when one tree is cut down another is planted in the same soil, so that when the spendthrift has run through his estate another possesses the inheritance and grows up from the very ground where he might have flourished. Clarke reports, only to reject, Mr. Good's ingenious turn of the second clause upon God himself — "behold the Eternal, exulting in his course; even over his dust shall raise up another" — a reading no ancient version supports and which, he judges, neither advances the argument nor suits the strong irony of the place, which he likens rather to the sardonic "rejoice, O young man, in thy youth" of Eccl. 11:9.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states it simply — this is the issue of the flourishing state, all his joy comes to this; and out of the same earth or place shall another tree grow. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets over the whole the psalmist's verdict that "the way of the ungodly shall perish" (Ps. 1:6): the hope the man thought would issue in joy issues instead in this, and his place is filled by others, nothing akin to him, who rule over that for which he laboured and are no more warned by his fall than he was by another's. The witnesses converge on the irony Bildad intends: that the "joy" of the wicked man's way is the very ruin that ends it.
20:
"Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will he help the evil doers" — Bildad now sums his whole speech in a maxim, and the witnesses receive the doctrine gladly while watching the use he makes of it. The reformed John Gill fastens on the comfort in the first clause: a perfect man is the sincere and upright man, not perfect in himself but in Christ, not by the completeness of his sanctification but by the perfection of his justification; and such a one God will never cast away — not out of his sight, whose name is graven on the palms of his hands, nor out of his heart's love, nor out of his covenant, nor out of the hands of his Son, nor so as to perish eternally. The promise, taken in itself, is one Gill will defend to the hilt.

The wesleyan-arminian voices take it as an ancient maxim honestly meant. Adam Clarke calls it another of the sayings of the fathers that Bildad produces — "as surely as God will punish and root out the wicked, so surely will he defend and save the righteous"; and John Wesley agrees that God, who will not help the evil-doer, will not cast away a good man, though he may be cast down. Yet Wesley at once marks the flaw: it may be that a good man will not be lifted up in this world, and therefore Bildad could not infer, from Job's not being restored to prosperity, that he was no good man.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays the false logic bare. Bildad assures Job that as he was, so he should fare, and thence concludes that as he fared, so he was — setting before him life and death, the blessing and the curse, and reading his present ruin backward into his character. It is true, Henry grants, that God will not cast away an upright man; he may be cast down for a time, but not cast away for ever, and if not in this world, then in another his mouth shall be filled with rejoicing. It is true, too, that God will not take the ungodly by the hand (as the margin reads), for what communion has light with darkness, and between them a great gulf is fixed (Luke 16:26). But it does not follow that because Job's family was sunk and himself for the present helpless, he was therefore an ungodly man; that is neither just nor charitable. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the sense of "help," reading it as the "taking by the hand" of one owned as God's own, and note how the close of the speech runs like a psalm. The witnesses converge: the maxim is golden, but Bildad's inference from it, that suffering convicts the sufferer, is the error the whole book was written to overthrow.
21:
Bildad's last words soften almost into a benediction, promising that God will "fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing," and the witnesses weigh both the warmth of the close and the condition tucked inside it. The reformed John Gill hears the promise addressed directly to Job: if he prove sincere and upright, God will not cast him away but help and restore him, and not leave him until his heart is so full of joy that mouth and lips break forth in strong expressions of it, as if it were a year of jubilee with him. Yet Gill will not miss the insinuation beneath the kindness — Bildad tacitly implies that Job is no perfect man but an evil-doer whom God has cast away, concluding it from his distressed circumstances, which is no rule of judgment at all, since love and hatred are not to be known by outward prosperity or adversity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers to read the two closing verses as a prayer — "even yet may he fill thy mouth with laughter!" — and grants that Bildad speaks with less virulence than Eliphaz, though with equal positiveness in the grand charge: that a man so afflicted must be a great sinner. This most exceptionable position, Clarke protests, is contrary to plain fact and founded only on maxims borrowed from the ancients; observation must have corrected it in a hundred instances, and the very history of the patriarchs refutes it — righteous Abel murdered by Cain, Abram driven from his country, Jacob persecuted by Esau, Joseph sold by his brothers, Moses a fugitive, and David and the prophets afflicted. The best of men are often in the deepest trouble; it is not by prosperity or adversity that we may read God's approval, for the true rule is our Lord's, "by their fruits ye shall know them" (Matt. 7:16).

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the line "he will yet fill thy mouth with laughter — afflicted though thou hast been, thou shalt again rejoice," and names the temper behind it as an unsympathetic selfishness: Bildad wishes to think well of his friend because he is his friend, but cannot reconcile his affliction with any theory of righteous government, and so is driven to suspect that all is not right with him, while still holding out the hope that if he casts away the secret sin all shall yet be well. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the "till" as pure encouragement — what has been said in general of good men shall be made good to Job if he is such, for God will not forsake him nor cease doing him good till he gives him abundant matter of rejoicing (v.20). The witnesses converge: the promise is fair and even tender, yet it hangs upon a suspicion the sufferer does not deserve.
22:
"They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame; and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought" — Bildad ends where he began, dividing the world into the vindicated and the ruined, and the witnesses read the double promise as the mirror of the maxim of v.20. The reformed John Gill takes "they that hate thee" for the Chaldeans and Sabeans who had plundered Job of his substance; when they should see him restored beyond all hope, and themselves liable to his resentment and under the displeasure of Providence, they would be covered with utter confusion — a shame as visible, the phrase implies, as the clothes upon a man's back.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his comment on the whole passage, hears both clauses together. Those who had triumphed in Job's fall would be ashamed of their insolence when they saw him restored; and it is true that the enemies of the saints will be clothed with shame when they behold them crowned with honour. As for the dwelling-place of the wicked coming to nought, Henry grants the certainty of it — sin brings ruin upon persons and families, and only those who make God their dwelling-place are safe for ever, while those who make other things their refuge are disappointed (Ps. 90:1). Yet he repeats his caution against Bildad's drift: to argue, as the friend slyly does, that because Job's house was fallen he must have been an ungodly man, was neither just nor charitable while no other evidence of his wickedness appeared.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley had already drawn the balance in the preceding verses — that God will not help the evil-doer, whose tent shall be no more, but neither will he finally cast away the good man, though he be cast down for a season, so that no conclusion against Job could fairly be built on his present ruin. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note only that this triumphant close, with its shamed enemies and vanished tent of the ungodly, sounds throughout like the language of the Psalms. The witnesses do not divide over the truth of the verse, that hatred of God's people ends in shame and that the refuge of the wicked comes to nothing; their whole reserve is for the sting in Bildad's application, which turns a psalm-like promise into one more quiet accusation, leaving Job, at the end of the second friend's speech, comforted with a hope he must earn by confessing a guilt he does not own.
